title: The Long Discourses, closed
hookLine: from a net that catches every view to a young man bowing in the street

cards: The first long discourse begins on a road. The Buddha and his monks are walking between two cities, and behind them walk a wandering teacher and his student, arguing. The teacher criticizes the Buddha the whole way.
The student praises him the whole way.
Early next morning the monks are buzzing about it, and the Buddha's first words in the whole collection are about that: if people speak against me, or against the teaching, don't get angry.
If they praise us, don't get puffed up. Just say what's true and what isn't. Fifty-odd days later, this path reaches the end of that road.

teach.h: SIXTY-TWO VIEWS CAUGHT IN A NET
teach.b: Look at the shape of the journey. It starts huge.
In that first discourse, the Buddha lays out sixty-two views about the self and the world, and says every such theory is caught among them, like fish in a fine net cast over a small pond.
Every one of them, he says, grows out of feeling and craving. It's a teaching about how minds build positions.

teach.h: KINGS, GODS AND THE LAST JOURNEY
teach.b: Then come the kings, the wanderers and the gods, and the long, slow walk of the last journey to the final words. And then the collection comes down to earth.

A young man named Sigala in the street at dawn, bowing to the directions because his father asked him to. The Buddha doesn't tell him to stop; he tells him what each bow could mean. Six ways money leaks.
How to know a real friend. And after the four kings' protective verses, it closes with Sariputta, counting the teaching aloud so it stays whole.

teach.h: FROM EVERY VIEW TO THE KITCHEN TABLE
teach.b: From the net of every view to how you treat the person who cleans your house.
That's the long way home: the biggest questions end up at the kitchen table. Tomorrow a new collection begins, much shorter, with poems some scholars count among the oldest Buddhist verses.

how: In Theravada monasteries the Digha Nikaya is studied, and some of its discourses, such as the advice to Sigala, are taught to lay people as a guide for daily life.

o: the supreme net that catches sixty-two views
a fishing net blessed by a brahmin priest
a hymn sung to Brahma at every sunrise

games.q: the long discourses, start to finish: tap the pairs.
p: sixty-two views caught in a net
bows to six directions at dawn

s: the Long Discourses open with the Buddha telling monks not to be angry at criticism
nor elated at praise; just say what is true and what isn't.
the net of views catches sixty-two views
every theory of the self and world the discourse can name, like fish in a fine net.
the collection ends with the Buddha's death
the last journey is DN 16; the collection ends with Sigala and Sariputta's lists.

games.q: you're one of the monks. all day a wandering teacher has criticized the Buddha on the road. that evening, what does the Buddha tell you?
o: don't be angry or elated; say what's true and what isn't.
games.why: the first long discourse opens with this: neither anger at blame nor pride at praise, only a calm account of what's true.

practice: Pick one long discourse, perhaps not yesterday's scene: the moonlit king, the last journey, Sigala's six directions, whichever comes.

Tell it to yourself in three beats, how it starts, what turns, how it ends, slowly, as if telling a child at bedtime, and if a gap appears, just notice it and go on. Then let the story go quiet and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: brahmajala. Thirty-four teachings, the Digha Nikaya, running from a net that catches every view to the duties of ordinary life. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali brahmajala: the supreme net, the name of DN 1, which catches sixty-two views.

carryVoice: Your line: the long way home. Every big question ends up at someone's table. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta: praise and blame; the net of sixty-two views
